title: Hanuman's first words
hook: honesty answered with honesty, and two princes carried up a mountain

segments.voice: Yesterday: Hanuman's first words, and Rama's praise for them: not one word wrong, not too long, not rushed.

Now it's Lakshmana's turn to answer, and he does something you might not expect from a wary prince in a dangerous forest. He tells the stranger everything. Who they are. Why they're in exile. That Sita has been taken by a rakshasa while they were away, and they don't know where. That Kabandha sent them to find Sugriva. A wary prince might give a stranger the short version. Lakshmana gives the whole thing.
screen: `LAKSHMANA ANSWERS.` → `HE TELLS IT ALL.` → `NOT THE SHORT VERSION.`

segments.voice: Trust answered with trust. Hanuman spoke carefully and honestly, and Lakshmana meets that honesty with his own. He even asks for help in so many words: Rama, who used to be a refuge for others, has now come to Sugriva for refuge. That's a humbling sentence for a prince of Ayodhya to say out loud, and Lakshmana says it. Hanuman hears it and is glad. Your aim and Sugriva's are the same, he says. Sugriva too has lost his wife and his kingdom to someone stronger. You can help each other. Then the disguise comes off. Hanuman drops the mendicant's form and takes his own shape: a monkey, the son of the Wind. And he does something lovely and practical. Rishyamuka is steep, and the brothers have walked a long way. So he lifts them both onto his shoulders and carries them up the mountain to Sugriva. As for his name: later in the epic, when the monkeys need to remind Hanuman who he is, the old bear Jambavan tells the story behind it. As a baby he leapt at the rising sun thinking it was a fruit, Indra's thunderbolt struck his jaw, his hanu, and so he was called Hanuman. Today we see something simpler. A minister who listened well and spoke well, then put two tired strangers on his shoulders and carried them uphill. Three days of first words, and they end not with a speech but with a lift.
screen: `TRUST ANSWERED WITH TRUST.` · `RAMA SEEKS REFUGE.` · `THE DISGUISE COMES OFF.` · `CARRIED UP THE MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: Let your shoulders drop, and feel how much they carry on an ordinary day: bags, children, worries, other people's moods. Breathe in and notice the weight; breathe out and let some of it slide off. If someone comes to mind whose load you could share, just hold them there for a moment.
Hanu, the jaw struck by Indra's thunderbolt, which gave Hanuman his name.
Your line: carried up the mountain. Honesty met honesty, and then came the lift. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Images of Hanuman carrying Rama and Lakshmana on his shoulders are common in Hindu art and temple sculpture, and some devotees speak of Hanuman as the one who carries others to Rama.

original.note: Sanskrit hanumān (hanumat): in Jambavan's story, named for his hanu, the jaw the thunderbolt struck.

trapdoor: what you thought: Hanuman shows up and the alliance is instant.
what it means: it's built step by step, honesty answered with honesty.
what a scholar hears: Kishkindha 4 has Lakshmana's account and Hanuman carrying the brothers; the sun-and-jaw story is told by Jambavan in Kishkindha 66 (and again in the Uttara Kanda).
recall: the sage who gave Rama Vishnu's bow
guess: the jaw, the part of the body behind a famous name
the wind god said to be the monkey's own father
the thunderbolt that Indra hurls at his enemies

chat.says: Hanuman carried Rama and Lakshmana up a mountain? Why would he do that?
options: They'd walked far up a steep slope, so he lifted them and carried them to Sugriva.
Rama was wounded from a battle with Ravana and couldn't walk on his own.
Hanuman wanted to show off his strength before agreeing to any friendship.
chat.meaning: After Lakshmana answers honestly, Hanuman drops his disguise and carries the tired brothers up Rishyamuka to Sugriva: trust answered with trust, then a lift.

Hanuman.meaning: son of the Wind, Sugriva's minister, devoted to Rama

Jambavan.meaning: the old bear who later tells Hanuman's birth story

Indra.meaning: king of the gods, whose thunderbolt struck baby Hanuman

Rishyamuka.meaning: the mountain where Sugriva hides from Vali

rakshasa.meaning: a demon; Ravana is the rakshasas' king

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda 4 (Lakshmana's answer; Hanuman carries the brothers)
Valmiki Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda 66 (Jambavan tells Hanuman's birth story)

notes: Sarga numbers follow the common (vulgate) numbering and differ between editions; confirm against the edition the Keeper uses.
The etymology of Hanuman (hanu, jaw) is the traditional explanation; scholars propose others. Confirm wording.
Lakshmana's line that Rama, once a refuge for others, now seeks refuge with Sugriva: paraphrased from Kishkindha 4; confirm.
Whether Lakshmana tells Hanuman that a rakshasa took Sita, and whether he names Ravana here: confirm. The script says only 'a rakshasa'.
